In the late Mr. Bosworth Smith's attractive book, " Bird Life and Bird Lore," a popular edition ef which was recently published by Mr. Murray, some interesting instances of "solitary" birds find mention. One is a heron which was to be see at Biagham's Molcombe. Noone ever observed this particular heron with or near a mate. No other heron was to be found even as a casual visitor within three or four miles of him. He had apparently no kith, no kin - although he had enemies, but as longas Mr. Smith knew him he managed to escape them. 'fhe brook which flows through the bottom of the manor house garden, and by which he generally took his stand, is a meagre one, very scantily supplied with fish, but there he was year in, year out.
